title: A spectral fit is not yet a free-light hypothesis
question: What can the low-frequency coefficient determine about molecular scale?
recap: Matching a spectral coefficient to classical thermal allocation constrains R/N. Quantized resonator energies and independently propagating light quanta are different claims.
premises: Both sides use the same spectral density and the same units.
The spectral constants and the gas constant are separate inputs to any inference drawn from them.
limitations: Modern exact SI constants give a consistency check, not a new measurement of N.
A fit to the Planck spectrum does not by itself establish independently moving light elements.

overview.text: Matching a spectral coefficient to classical thermal allocation constrains R/N. Quantized resonator energies and independently propagating light quanta are different claims.

full.text: Write the historical spectral constants as \(A\) and \(B\) in this explanatory notation. At low \(\nu/T\), expanding the exponential denominator gives a term proportional to \(\nu^2 T\). Its coefficient can be compared to the classical allocation from §1.

full.spoken: At low frequency relative to temperature, the spectrum approaches A over B times frequency squared times temperature.
Equating the coefficients gives N equal to B over A times eight pi R over light speed cubed.

full.text: This comparison is about coefficients and their experimental provenance. In the modern SI, \(R\) equals \(N_A k_B\). Inserting that identity and the modern spectral constants recovers the defined \(N_A\); it is not independent evidence for a molecular count.
Planck’s resonators belong to the matter that emits or absorbs radiation. Einstein’s proposed energy elements concern the radiation itself. Moving between those statements requires an argument.

full.returnCaption: Return to matching the two spectral coefficients.

steps.returnCaption: Return to the hydrogen atom's 1.62 × 10⁻²⁴ gram and the number N.

steps.text: Letters as printed: the paper writes Planck's two constants as α and β, and this explanation names them A and B. Here β divides a frequency by a temperature inside an exponential, so it is a constant of the radiation law, Wien's constant; it is not the relativity paper's β. L, written c below, is the speed of light.

steps.spoken: At low frequency relative to temperature, the spectrum approaches A over B times frequency squared times temperature.

items: This has the same form as the classical allocation of §1, \(\frac{R}{N}\frac{8\pi\nu^2}{L^3}T\): both are a constant times \(\nu^2T\). For the two to agree at every low frequency and every temperature, the constants in front must be equal.
Set them equal, then multiply both sides by N and by B/A to leave N alone.

steps.spoken: Equating the coefficients gives N equal to B over A times eight pi R over light speed cubed.

items: Worked with the paper's inputs. The page prints β as \(4{,}866\cdot10^{-11}\) and α as \(6{,}10\cdot10^{-56}\). The provenance receipt records the exponent of α as a misprint, and this edition computes with \(A=6.10\times10^{-57}\).

R and L are not printed as numbers in §2. With the standard values of 1905, \(R=8.31\times10^{7}\) erg per kelvin per gram-molecule and \(L=3\times10^{10}\) cm per second, supplied as inputs: B/A is \(7.98\times10^{45}\), \(8\pi R/L^3\) is \(7.74\times10^{-23}\), and their product is \(N=6.17\times10^{23}\).
The page prints \(N=6{,}17\cdot10^{23}\), and adds that one atom of hydrogen weighs 1/N gram. Check it: \(1/(6.17\times10^{23})=1.62\times10^{-24}\) gram, the number the page gives.
The misprinted exponent cannot be the one used: the same arithmetic with \(6.10\times10^{-56}\) gives \(6.17\times10^{22}\), ten times smaller than the number printed.

The paper notes that this is the value Planck found, and that it agrees satisfactorily with values found by other routes. Its point is narrower than it may look: Planck's determination of N depends only to a degree on his theory of radiation, because only the long-wavelength form of the spectrum enters.

The conclusion the paper draws from §§1 and 2: its theoretical foundations serve better the greater the energy density and the wavelength of the radiation, and fail completely for short wavelengths and small densities. §4 works in exactly that region.
Keep the evidence straight. In today's SI, R is defined as \(N_Ak_B\), so putting modern constants into this formula returns the defined \(N_A\) and tests nothing about molecules.

Keep the two claims apart. Planck's resonators belong to the matter that emits and absorbs; the energy elements the paper goes on to propose belong to the radiation itself. Getting from one to the other takes the argument of §§3 to 6.

steps.returnCaption: Return to matching the two spectral coefficients.

margin.text: The paper writes the spectral constants as \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\); \(A\) and \(B\) here are editorial names for them. In §2 Einstein derives \(N = 6.17 \times 10^{23}\) from Planck’s printed constants. The historical constant set reproduces that number and the modern set does not, so the two are kept apart.
